title: Meta Pauses Zuckerberg Share Plan During Investor Legal Fight
detail:
Meta Pauses Zuckerberg Share Plan During Investor Legal Fight
Signage outside Meta headquarters in Menlo Park, California. · Bloomberg · Bloomberg

(Bloomberg) -- Meta Platforms Inc. said it will hold off on distributing a new class of shares while a legal fight plays out with investors who oppose the tech giant's plan to fund the company's artificial intelligence investments without diluting Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg's stake.

The plan called for Meta to create a new category of non-voting Class C shares on Jan. 19 that would be issued later as a dividend to existing investors, including Zuckerberg. The arrangement would also allow Zuckerberg, Meta's co-founder and the world's fifth-richest person, to sell some of that stock without reducing his majority voting power.

In a court filing Wednesday, Meta agreed to hold off issuing any Class C shares during the legal fight, which is set for trial in Delaware Chancery Court in April.

"In the best interest of our shareholders, we are seeking a final determination as quickly as the court will allow, and we will vigorously defend against these claims," Meta said in a statement.

The company has said the new share class is critical to helping it raise capital needed to build out AI infrastructure to compete in the race to dominate that field, and that it must move quickly because companies are being shut out of the bond market to finance investments.

The Class C plan will give Zuckerberg more leeway in how he manages his fortune because he can more easily sell his stake in Meta for cash. It also would have helped him pay a proposed wealth tax on California billionaires that was recently rejected by 53% of voters in a referendum.

Meta's plan has prompted 10 shareholder lawsuits against Zuckerberg and other board members in Delaware Chancery Court for allegedly breaching their fiduciary duties by pushing through a deal the investors claim is unfair. Those cases have now been consolidated in one action.

"Public stockholders receive a pro rata stock dividend, but no corresponding governance protection or vote on the transaction," wrote attorneys for plaintiffs in one of the suits. "They also bear the economic and market costs of the new non-voting class and remain unable to influence most corporate decisions."

Meta earlier announced that board approval of the deal came after "the unanimous recommendation of a special committee of disinterested and independent directors" and that it was "in the best interests of Meta and its shareholders."

Today's big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036?

Booking Holdings (BKNG) expects its room nights to grow 1% to 3% in the fourth quarter of 2026. Management gave that guidance on its November 3, 2026 call. Room nights are the nights travelers book through its sites. They offer the plainest count of the travel Booking sells. The guidance would mark a clear slowdown from the third quarter. So why is Booking expecting room-night growth to slow?

Why Booking Holdings Expects Slower Room-Night Growth

Management gave two reasons for the slower growth. Booking faces its toughest year-earlier comparison of 2026. It is also unsure how recent events will affect travel demand. In October, demand was hit by disrupted travel to and from the Middle East, elevated airfares and localized unrest in certain European cities. Management's guide assumes the effects of the Middle East conflict last through the end of the year.

Room nights grew 7% in the third quarter, accelerating from 5% in the second quarter and topping management's own guidance.

Booking also expects slower sales growth and flat profit. Management expects adjusted revenue, the company's own measure, to grow 0% to 2% in the fourth quarter, after rising 9% in the third. It expects adjusted EBITDA, a profit measure, to be about flat from a year earlier. Part of the reason is that it plans to spend more on flights, attractions, dining and AI.

Will Booking Holdings' Slowdown Last Into 2027?

Management has not said yet. The company plans to discuss 2027 in February with its fourth-quarter results. Executives did offer early signs on both sides.

On the hopeful side, management said its on-the-book statistics for the first half of 2027 look healthy. It called them a very early indicator, still subject to cancellations. Booking's alternative accommodation listings grew 9% in the third quarter. Management called that an encouraging signal for future growth in that category.

On the other side, management said travel demand was resilient in the third quarter but moderated somewhat toward its end. How long the slowdown lasts remains an open question for holders.

How Hard Has Booking Holdings Stock Been Hit?

Booking Holdings stock has lost 22.8% over the past year, against a 10.3% gain for the S&P 500. The shares trade at 16.1 times earnings, against 22.0 for the S&P 500. At the end of September, before the outlook, Booking's P/E was already the second lowest of 40 quarter ends since December 2016. Today's 16.1 is lower still, so the price likely assumes slower growth ahead.

Warning for Meta Investors: Muse "Has to Be 20x" What It Is Now to Make an Impact, Says Dan Nathan ©Изображения пользователя Maximusnd Zahar from Canva
Key Takeaways

Meta says more than 10 million people set up Muse in about six weeks, but Dan Nathan says that number has to be 20x larger to make an impact.

Each new Muse user adds compute cost for Meta before it adds revenue, and that cost is revenue for its chip suppliers.

Analysts expect Meta's free cash flow to fall to negative $48.2 billion in 2027.

Muse won't move Meta's numbers for years, and the fourth-quarter call in late January is the next test of its costs and its first revenue.

Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) says more than 10 million people set up Muse, its AI personal agent, in about six weeks. Dan Nathan, co-founder of RiskReversal Media, isn't impressed. On today's episode of the RiskReversal Pod, he said "that number has to be 20x what it is right now to make an impact."

His bigger worry is the cost: "So if they can't monetize it, the bigger it gets, meaning like the more folks that are using it, it's the more money they're going to lose on the thing." Meta pays chipmakers like Broadcom (AVGO:NASDAQ) and AMD (AMD:NASDAQ) for the buildout behind that compute, and they get paid whether Muse makes money or not.

Every user costs money first

Management expects Muse's total serving costs to rise as users grow, and calls the service compute-intensive. Meta pays for that out of free cash flow, which analysts expect to swing from $43.6 billion in 2025 to negative $48.2 billion in 2027:

Meta Platforms (META): free cash flow, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2023-2028 (TIKR)

The reason is capital spending, which nearly doubled to $69.7 billion in 2025:

Meta Platforms (META): capital expenditures, $ billions, fiscal 2021-2025 (TIKR)

Meta's 2026 capex guidance is $135 billion to $145 billion, including finance-lease principal, and analysts expect about $210 billion in 2027. Not all of that is Muse, since the same compute runs Meta's ad-ranking models. But Muse is the part with no revenue line yet.

TIKR tracks 62 analysts on Meta Platforms. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Meta Platforms, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Meta Platforms' Analyst Ratings

20x is a tall order

Nathan's 20x would put Muse at 200 million users. Set that against Meta's revenue, which analysts expect to reach $313 billion in 2027:

Meta Platforms (META): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2023-2028 (TIKR)

For Muse to bring in just 1% of that, about $3.1 billion, today's 10 million users would each have to bring in about $313 a year. At 200 million users, it's about $16 each, roughly a quarter of the $57 Meta made per person across its apps in 2025.

And Muse is only live in the US and Canada, partly because of compute cost, so getting to 200 million probably means taking on more of that cost.

title: Meta’s hope to grow ‘school communities’ was really just a push to get teens hooked, internal docs show
detail:
Meta’s hope to grow ‘school communities’ was really just a push to get teens hooked, internal docs show
Isabel Keane
Wed, November 18, 2026 at 10:47 AM MST 4 min read
META
Trade META on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Meta's push to grow "school communities" and provide a safer experience on Instagram for children in the United States was also a ploy to get more teens joining the social media platform, according to a report.

The social media giant launched "Project Gryffindor," a "school partnership program," in 2025. The program was meant to connect students, parents and the school community, encouraging children to use their school banner on their profile and establishing a student directory.

By this September, nearly 17,000 schools had signed up for the program, according to internal Meta documents obtained by NPR. The project's name is taken from the Harry Potter books, with Gryffindor one of four school houses at Hogwarts.

Meta said its program was to provide a safer experience on Instagram for children, and to prevent bullying. It also served as a way for parents and students to stay informed on things happening at school.

However, internal company documents showed that Meta discussed other motivations for establishing the school networks, including that it was a way to increase user "acquisition," "friending" and "invites" to join Instagram.

Meta said its program was to provide a safer experience on Instagram for children, and to prevent bullying. It also served as a way for parents and students to stay informed on things happening at school. However, internal company documents showed that Meta discussed other motivations for establishing the school networks, including that it was a way to increase user 'acquisition' (AP)

"We believe network connections will fuel organic and unattributed acquisition," stated a presentation, used internally, in reference to new users joining Instagram.

In another internal presentation from 2023, that was obtained by NPR, Meta stated that its school program would "give teens a new reason to join / find more value in IG [Instagram]."

"Our current strategy of relying on power user teens to get less active friends onto IG may not be effective if there are full communities of teens that have not yet joined IG," the presentation stated.

The internal Meta documents were obtained through discovery as part of a multi-district lawsuit alleging that social media platforms are designed to be harmful for users under-18. The lawsuit also alleges that social media companies are aware their products have risks that they fail to disclose to users. Meta, TikTok, Google and Snap are all named as defendants in the suit.

Children participating in Instagram's school partnership program may also be at greater risk of being targeted by predators or scammers, despite the company's claims about making the platform safer for kids, experts told NPR.

"There's nothing to say that you know a student's account can't get hacked and then taken by a criminal and then used for all sorts of nefarious purposes, whether it be sextortion, grooming," cybersecurity investigators Paul Raffile told NPR. "Once an account is embedded within a school and has an active school profile, they can see all sorts of things like directories of the different clubs, different groups on campus, and that's a sextortionist's dream."

Nvidia reported results on Tuesday after the close. Sales were $115.8 billion in the quarter to October, double a year ago. Nvidia's outlook for the January quarter is $130 billion. The stock closed Tuesday at $155.46, down 0.4%, before the report.

Most coverage will focus on those two numbers. This article looks at a different one: what customers owe.

On Tuesday morning, Could Nvidia Stock Fall 50%? Follow The Cash named three lines to read in this report. They were operating cash, receivables and investment gains. Here is how each one came in.

Did The Cash Catch Up?

Mostly, yes. In the quarter to October, Nvidia booked $65.3 billion of profit. It took in $48.3 billion of cash from its operations. That is 74% of its profit. In July, it was 40%.

Free cash flow is the cash left after capital spending. It was $43.8 billion, more than double July's $21.4 billion.

That removes one of the worst cases in Tuesday's article. That case used Nvidia's free cash flow at July's pace. It applied the price investors paid for each dollar of free cash at the December 2018 low. The result was about $83 a share. At October's pace, the same price gives about $170. That is above Tuesday's close.

One quarter of cash moved that value for Nvidia from about $83 a share to about $170. If Nvidia is a big part of your wealth, so are its risk and its tax bill. So Why Do Customers Owe $81 Billion?

This is the line that got worse. Receivables are money customers owe for chips already delivered. At Nvidia, they rose to $81.0 billion at the end of the October quarter, from $63.1 billion in July. That is $18.0 billion more in one quarter.

To compare across years, we turn receivables into days of sales: receivables divided by the quarter's sales, times 91 days. By that measure, customers owed about 64 days of sales. That is up from 60 in July and 45 in April.

Nvidia's own record goes back to 2001. In that time, customers owed it more than 64 days of sales in only three quarters. The closest case below those is October 2018, at 63 days.

Today's big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036?

Two weeks ago we asked where a 2022-size chip-stock fall would take Nvidia. That 46% fall pointed to about $129 (Nvidia Stock To $129?).

On Tuesday the stock closed at $155.46. That is 35% below its October 6 peak of $239.24. After the close, Nvidia reported its biggest quarter yet: $65.3 billion of profit on $115.8 billion of sales. Is it cheap now? We check its own history, on profit and on cash.

Is Nvidia Cheap?

On profit, yes, by its own history. In the four quarters through the October quarter reported Tuesday, Nvidia earned $226.3 billion, or $9.31 a share. At Tuesday's close, the stock traded at 16.7 times that profit. This ratio is the P/E: the price divided by the last four quarters' profit per share.

At its December 24, 2018 low, after the crypto-mining boom ended, investors paid 17.0 times. No month-end since August 2013 had a P/E this low.

How Often Has Nvidia Been This Cheap?

Rarely, and not lately. We looked at 287 month-ends since December 2002. Nvidia traded at 18 times its trailing profit or less in 42 of them. Only one came after July 2015: December 2018, at 17.8. The table shows where the stock stood 12 months later.

A low P/E was not a good signal on its own. After the 42 cheap month-ends, the stock was higher a year later 31 times, with a median gain of 22%. After the other 233, it was higher 182 times, with a median gain of 52%.

A low P/E has not been a buy signal on its own. If you are waiting for a better price, your cash does not have to sit idle. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3x the S&P 500's, from 50 stocks with at least 10 straight years of dividends. See what it pays.

What decided each year was what profit and cash did next. In February 2008, Nvidia traded at 16.4 times profit. Within a year, its trailing profit went from $0.80 billion to a small loss. The stock fell 61%.

After December 2018, trailing profit fell almost by half, to $2.41 billion by October 2019. Yet the stock rose 77%. In the four quarters before that low, cash had kept pace with profit. Operating cash, the cash the business brings in, was 90% of profit.
